item.title: 'Dallas’ star Patrick Duffy says mother was killed rushing to husband after gunmen opened fire at bar
item.description: Patrick Duffy described how his father took a step toward the returning gunmen before they opened fire, killing both parents in their Montana bar.
item.content:encoded:
Patrick Duffy's mother was doing a crossword puzzle when two armed men returned to the bar she and her husband owned in Montana, and one of them shot her husband. Moments later, she rushed toward him and was shot and killed, too.

The "Dallas" star, 77, recalled the final moments of his parents' lives during an appearance on the "Still Here Hollywood" podcast, revealing how the double murder unfolded and how he found the strength to carry on.

The murders took place nearly 40 years ago, on Nov. 18, 1986.

'DALLAS' STAR PATRICK DUFFY AND LINDA PURL RECALL START OF SURPRISING LOVE STORY: 'BOTH NERVOUS AS TEENAGERS'

"My parents were murdered when two young men robbed the bar that my parents owned in Montana," the actor told host Steve Kmetko. "My dad had thrown these two boys out because they were drunk and obstreperous. He just threw them out of the bar, and they went somewhere, finished whatever they were drinking, and the anger boiled up and they went back in."

Sean A. Wentz and Kenneth A. Miller were both 19 at the time, People magazine reported. Duffy's parents, Marie and Terence, were the only ones in the bar when the gunmen returned.

"It was very late at night," Duffy said. "There was nobody in the bar except my father and my mother, and they walked in with their shotguns. As soon as my dad saw them, this is in the testimony that came out in the court, my dad turned to them and apparently took a step towards them, saying, 'I told you to ...'"

WATCH: PATRICK DUFFY AND LINDA PURL FELL IN LOVE ONLINE

Duffy's father never finished his sentence.

"... That's when they opened up on him and killed him," Duffy said. "And then my mother was on the other end of the bar doing a crossword puzzle and took a couple steps running towards dad. And they shot her too."

"And then, if that wasn't stupid enough, instead of just running, they jumped over the bar to the cash register, took the money and a couple of bottles of booze and then left."

The Los Angeles Times previously reported that Terence and Marie's bodies were found by a group of people who had stopped for a drink after finishing their shifts at the nearby Montana Developmental Center. One woman spotted Marie on the floor but initially thought she might have fainted. When she saw blood on Terence, she went outside and flagged down a friend for help.

Duffy learned of his parents' deaths the following morning.

"... My sister had called she was completely devastated," he recalled. "... She was a police woman, and she was on her way to Montana. By the time I hung up the phone, there were film crews at the gate."

Duffy said Lorimar Television, the production company behind "Dallas," arranged transportation and other support for him following the murders.

"Lorimar [Television] called, everybody called, [the] support team got in there and said, 'We have the jet ready. We'll fly you to Montana. We'll take care of everything. We'll send a PR person with you to take care of all that.'"

Duffy said his Buddhist faith helped him cope with the loss. It also gave him the strength to tell his sons, Padraic and Conor, that their grandparents had been killed.

"The Buddhist philosophy is one of the continuous life cycle of your entity," Duffy explained on the podcast. 

"... The first thing I did was, it was just as the boys were getting up to go to school, very young, and I said, '... I'm going to chant with you,' because we always chanted before they went off to school. I said, 'We have to chant for grandma and grandpa because they've both been killed, and we have to chant for them because they're going to understand it and hear it.'"

Miller and Wentz were convicted in connection with the murders and sentenced to prison, according to People magazine. Nine.com.au reported that Miller was released on parole in 2007, and Wentz was granted parole in 2015.

Duffy previously told Closer Weekly that he still remembered his parents as "pretty ordinary, pleasant people" who were "very social" before the murders.

"When my parents were murdered, I went through all the emotions of the horrific event — shock and anger and everything — but I never felt disconnected from [my parents]," Duffy said. "I never felt that immediate loss. I did not know why then, but in retrospect, it was a result of being Buddhist."

"There was something about the eternity of life that had set deep inside me," he also told People magazine in 2020. "As horrific as that was, I didn't feel disconnected from them."

item.title: Minnesota Wild's Brock Faber to make season debut just seven weeks after suffering skull fracture
item.description: Brock Faber is set for his season debut with the Minnesota Wild just seven weeks after undergoing surgery for a skull fracture in the preseason.
item.content:encoded:
Minnesota Wild defenseman and member of the gold medal-winning USA men's hockey team Brock Faber is gearing up for his season debut, less than two months after suffering a skull fracture.

Faber has been out of action since the preseason, when the Wild played their final tune-up game against the Dallas Stars.

A shot from Dallas' Miro Heiskanen hit Faber in the head, and he went down in a heap.

He was able to skate off under his own power, but it was later revealed that the 24-year-old had undergone surgery for a fractured skull just days before the start of the season.

That's a horrific injury, so it's no shocker that Faber missed time. However, The Athletic's Michael Russo reported that he's ready to return to action just seven weeks later.

Yet another example of how NHL players are simply built different.

Hynes also said he expects to have Faber all in on special teams as well, getting time on both the power play and penalty kill.

item.title: Democrats push back across the nation after voters approve girls' sports protections
item.description: Proposition 318 and similar transgender school sports bans passed in four states, but Democratic leaders in Washington and Colorado push back.
item.content:encoded:
The battle over girls' sports is moving from ballot boxes to courtrooms as the years-long national debate has gotten a new wrinkle this month.

Democrats are turning Election Day victories for the "save women's sports" movement into fresh fights to reject the will of American voters.

Voters in four states approved measures restricting transgender participation in school sports this month, but Democratic leaders in Washington and Colorado are either backing court challenges or considering changes to what voters passed.

JACKSON THOMPSON: WASHINGTON STATE DEMOCRATIC PARTY CALLS GIRLS' SPORTS INITIATIVE UNCONSTITUTIONAL

The results highlight a divide between approval at the ballot box and acceptance among political leaders, even as some officials and athletic administrators commit to following the new laws.

Washington’s Initiative 638 passed with roughly 56% support. It prohibits biological males from competing in female school sports and requires students seeking to participate in girls’ athletics to provide healthcare documentation verifying their sex.

The Washington State Democratic Party quickly made clear that it supported continued resistance.

"The fight over I-638 is just beginning," the party said in a Nov. 6 statement.

The party argued the initiative violates the constitution and endorsed organizations planning court challenges.

The ACLU of Washington, Legal Voice and Pacifica Law Group subsequently sued on behalf of the state teachers union, a nonprofit and parents. The lawsuit argues that the measure discriminates against transgender girls and imposes unequal privacy burdens on girls seeking to play school sports.

The challengers seek to prevent the initiative from taking effect Dec. 3.

Seattle’s school board separately authorized legal action over the measure, citing concerns about privacy, equal treatment and conflicts with existing protections. That authorization allows the district to pursue legal action; it does not itself suspend the initiative.

Democratic Attorney General Nick Brown, meanwhile, appointed outside law firm Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner to defend the law on the state’s behalf.

"My personal views do not dictate what laws get defended or the strength of that defense," Brown said.

ADF SEEKS TO DEFEND WASHINGTON GIRLS' SPORTS MEASURE, ARGUES STATE CANNOT FULLY REPRESENT FEMALE ATHLETES

Brown said the arrangement would ensure the initiative receives a defense while allowing his office to continue its other work protecting transgender rights.

Alliance Defending Freedom filed a motion on behalf of Female Athletes United to defend Washington’s voter-approved girls sports initiative against an ACLU-backed lawsuit, arguing that the state cannot adequately represent the athletes’ interests, on Friday.

The Nov. 13 motion asks King County Superior Court to allow Female Athletes United to join the case as a defendant to defend Initiative 638. The request seeks the court’s permission to participate; it is not an order granting intervention.

In Colorado, voters approved Proposition 134 with approximately 52% support, requiring school and college sports teams to be designated male, female or coeducational and generally tying participation to biological sex.

Democratic Gov.-elect Phil Weiser has already signaled an interest in changing the measure.

"We’re going to have to take a look at these anti-trans measures and what adjustments are necessary and appropriate," Weiser said after the election, according to reporting by The Colorado Sun published by Colorado Public Radio.

Weiser raised concerns about potentially invasive eligibility verification. The measure does not expressly require genital examinations or establish a uniform statewide verification process.

He had not outlined specific changes in the reporting reviewed. Because Proposition 134 changes state law rather than the constitution, lawmakers can amend it without another statewide vote.

Demonstrators in Denver have demanded repeal. Supporters, including Protect Kids Colorado, have accused Weiser of disregarding the electorate’s decision.

Colorado’s athletic administrators have taken a more direct position on compliance.

"Like every member school, CHSAA must comply with the new law," a Colorado High School Activities Association spokesperson told Colorado Public Radio.

Denver Public Schools also said it would support students while following state law. The measure is scheduled to take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

Arizona voters approved Proposition 318 with approximately 59% support, expanding an existing law restricting male participation in girls’ sports.

The legislature referred the measure to voters with Republican support and Democratic opposition. Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs had vetoed similar legislation in previous years.

The proposition also restricts access to bathrooms, locker rooms and other private spaces based on sex recorded on an original birth certificate. It removes an existing provision allowing girls to participate on boys’ teams.

A pre-election lawsuit challenged the proposal, but a judge rejected the argument that it violated the single-subject rule and allowed it to remain on the ballot.

Opposition continued after passage. The ACLU of Arizona condemned the result, arguing that the measure further excludes transgender students.

"Lawmakers showed they would rather villainize vulnerable groups than defend our rights when they sent bad policies to the ballot, and unfortunately, some of those measures passed." said Victoria López, executive director for the ACLU of Arizona. "Proposition 317 will do nothing to make border communities safer, and risks labeling U.S. citizens and people seeking asylum as ‘terrorist organizations,’ Proposition 318 broadens an existing ban targeting trans student athletes to further ostracize kids who simply want to participate alongside their peers."

That statement did not announce a new lawsuit against Proposition 318. The absence of an announced post-election Democratic effort to block it should not be confused with an endorsement by Democrats who opposed it.

Nebraska’s Initiative 442 received roughly 68% support, placing restrictions on male participation in female school and college sports into the state constitution.

A voter guide published by the Nebraska Democratic Party recommended voting against it.

The proposal also survived a pre-election legal challenge. The Nebraska Supreme Court ruled Oct. 16 that the petition’s statement of purpose satisfied state requirements, rejecting an effort to keep the measure off the ballot.

The ACLU of Nebraska criticized the result after passage and said it would monitor potential harassment and discrimination against students. Its statement did not announce a new lawsuit.

Unlike Colorado’s statutory measure, Nebraska’s constitutional amendment cannot be undone through an ordinary legislative amendment. It reinforces a sports restriction already established in state law.

item.title: Bruce Buffer recalls wildest UFC brawls in and out of octagon, has strong words for banned Dillon Danis
item.description: Bruce Buffer recalls the Khabib Nurmagomedov and Conor McGregor cage brawl and shares his take on the Merab Dvalishvili hotel ambush in Abu Dhabi.
item.content:encoded:
Mixed martial artists are generally not friendly inside or outside of the octagon.

Brawls between fighters away from their fights are hardly a foreign concept, and there was another one in Abu Dhabi last week.

Former UFC bantamweight champion Merab Dvalishvili was jumped by MMA free agent Usman Nurmagomedov, the younger brother of Dvalishvili's former opponent, Umar Nurmagomedov, in a hotel lobby overseas. Usman Nurmagomedov and his crew were sentenced to six months in prison.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Bruce Buffer has been the ring announcer since 1996, so he's seen his fair share of scary moments.

"I was at the Khabib [Nurmagomedov] and Conor McGregor fight when Khabib jumped over the cage. That was a big deal. I’ve also seen other brawls break out. I’ve seen so many; I’ve been doing this for 31 years," Buffer recalled in a recent interview with OutKick. (Ironically, Khabib Nurmagomedov is Usman and Umar's cousin.)

UFC will head to Madison Square Garden on Saturday, and the last time MSG hosted fights, Dillon Dannis got into a brawl with several of lightweight champion Islam Makhachev's team in the stands. That event got him banned from UFC, which Buffer is more than fine with.

UFC RING ANNOUNCER BRUCE BUFFER, 69, HAS NO PLANS OF RETIREMENT ANY TIME SOON; WANTS 'TO KEEP GOING'

"Dylan’s banned. Dylan should be banned. It seems every time Dylan goes somewhere, he causes trouble, so there’s no reason for him to be anywhere near us. I have no problem saying that," Buffer said.

Buffer then remembers another brawl that had occurred after UFC 13 in 1997.

"I remember a big brawl in the early days at an after-party. I was talking to Tank Abbott, and all of a sudden I saw Tank get hit across the face with an overhand right. It was Wallid Ismail, and all hell broke loose," Buffer said.

"When I’m in a brawl like that, I get my back to a wall so you only have to worry about who’s in front of you. Everybody’s going at it. Always keep your back protected and know where your exit is. Know where your six is. Just watch. But things happen."

Buffer said he was "sorry to see" that Dvalishvili got fined, "because it wasn't his fault."

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

"But those are the laws over there. Don’t do anything - don’t throw punches unless you’re in the ring or the Octagon," he said. "If you’re in Abu Dhabi, it’s not going to be a good outcome."

item.title: Kim Kardashian poses in barely-there knit beach dress with fans calling her 'the most beautiful woman'

The 46-year-old reality star and businesswoman took to Instagram to share a series of photos of herself on the beach in a revealing knit dress that left much of her body exposed.

The dress featured a high neckline and beading, with the focal point being a number of cutouts that showed off her chest and torso.

The look also featured matching chunky knit armbands. She kept her makeup neutral, and let her long black hair flow in the wind as she posed for selfies on the shore.

SHAKIRA SOAKS UP THE MIAMI SUN AS BIKINI-CLAD NINA DOBREV, KIM KARDASHIAN SHOWCASE SUMMER GETAWAYS

item.title: Boise State head coach provides a refreshing, faith-filled College GameDay interview
item.description: Spencer Danielson's faith-focused responses on ESPN College GameDay in Boise Idaho ignited the crowd and drew massive praise from fans online.
item.content:encoded:
It's been 16 years since ESPN's College GameDay made its way to Boise, Idaho. Since the Broncos joined the FBS in 1996, they are in the top five for most wins with Ohio State, Alabama, Georgia, and Oklahoma. They have the most well-known playing surface in the sport: The iconic blue field. They are a Group of 6 powerhouse with the nation's leading rusher in Dylan Riley. Today, just like they did 16 years ago when College GameDay came to town, Boise State plays Oregon State.

College GameDay is always a lively, electric atmosphere, where the host team usually has their head coach speak with the panel of Pat McAfee, Rece Davis, Kirk Herbstreit, Desmond Howard and legendary coach Nick Saban during the broadcast. Saturday morning was no different.

Broncos Head Coach Spencer Danielson, who played linebacker and later coached for the then Division II Christian college out of Southern California, Azusa Pacific University, joined the panel, turning heads not only with his age (38) and positivity, but his faith-focused responses.

THE NFL IS AMERICA'S MOST GOD-CENTERED PROFESSIONAL SPORTS LEAGUE AND SUNDAY'S GAMES CONTINUED TO PROVE IT

In front of a sea of Boise State blue and orange, Danielson proclaimed as he answered Rece Davis's initial question, "First off, I appreciate all of you guys being here. And for me, man, always, thank you Jesus. We serve a God who's faithful."

As he said this, the crowd erupted.

Danielson wrapped up prefacing his answer by saying, "With God, all things are possible."

This echoed what Danielson said on Friday when he joined the "The Pat McAfee Show":

"I thank Jesus for the opportunity to be here because I’m not that smart, I’m not that cool. The only reason I’m the head coach is because Jesus put me here."

40 DAYS FOR LIFE CEO SHAWN CARNEY ON 'COLLEGE GAMEDAY' RELIGIOUS SIGN BAN: 'NOBODY'S FOR THIS'

In case you weren't aware of Coach Danielson and the way he conducts himself in interviews, this is nothing new. Many interviews start with a thankfulness to and praising of Jesus.

After securing their third straight Mountain West Championship in 2025, Danielson told Robert Griffin III, "First off, always, thank you Jesus. Faith doesn’t make things easy. It makes it possible. With God, all things are possible."

His statements on College GameDay received praise from many college football fans online.

"In the era of Godlessness we need more people like Coach Danielson," one X user said.

"Another reason I love Boise St."

"Spencer Danielson does this in every interview. Pay attention. Something extraordinary continues to happen in sports."

Danielson added in his interview with the College GameDay panel, "The only reason I'm here is Jesus."

He also said, "I know I'm here by [God's] grace and I wanna have an impact on these kids."

When you watch the game on Saturday evening, you'll hear much of the same from Coach Danielson.

item.title: Kentucky coach Mark Pope gives insanely tone-deaf answer after Wildcats nearly lose as 30-point favorites
item.description: Mark Pope told Rupp Arena fans he hopes they "had fun" after Kentucky needed a near-miracle to escape Northern Arizona 78-77 as 30-point favorites.
item.content:encoded:
With all the upheaval caused by the FAA ground stop on Friday evening, it's easy to forget there were plenty of intriguing sporting events taking place to provide an appetizer to a weekend of great football.

For example, college basketball is now in full swing and one game between a perennial power and a winless mid-major gave everyone a surprisingly drama-filled ending.

The Kentucky Wildcats are one of the bluest bloods in the sport, but their season was already off to a shaky start coming into Friday's matchup with the Northern Arizona Lumberjacks.

Big Blue Nation has already had to endure a scare against James Madison and a 20-point beatdown at the hands of the Kansas Jayhawks, but nothing could have prepared these Wildcat fans for what was to come in Rupp Arena against an 0-3 NAU squad.

My buddy Dan Zaksheske wrote an entire piece about the game itself, so check that out if you're interested, but suffice to say, Kentucky needed a near-miracle to escape against the visiting Lumberjacks.

What's worse, the Wildcats were 30-point favorites against Northern Arizona; this was supposed to be a "get right" game.

Instead, Kentucky needed a couple of front-end misses from a pair of one-and-one opportunities at the free throw line from its opponent and some Rupp magic to squeak out a 78-77 "victory."

COLLEGE BASKETBALL PLAYER'S BIZARRE FOUL SHOT GOES VIRAL IN SEASON-OPENER: 'DIABOLICAL'

It hardly felt like a win to all the fans in attendance, and just as the loyal folks of Big Blue Nation were trying to make sense of what just happened, the most tone-deaf man in America was giving a postgame news conference.

"I hope everyone in Rupp had fun."

IS IT WEIRD FOR A COACH TO NOT TALK TO HIS TEAM AFTER A GAME, OR IS IT EXTREMELY WEIRD?

Are you insane?

For context, that man is Mark Pope, head basketball coach for the University of Kentucky.

If you thought maybe that was the Northern Arizona coach, you would be forgiven, because in no world should a coach at a royally blue-blooded program like Kentucky ever say something like that after his $20 million roster just got worked by a mid-major.

He's lucky they didn't fire him right after the presser was over.

KENTUCKY COACH WILL STEIN TELLS WILDCATS PLAYERS 'IF YOU DON'T BELIEVE IN WHAT WE'RE DOING, YOU ARE HIGH'

"It's really entertaining," he said, without a hint of irony. "I think this will be a fun team to follow."

Yeah, for Tennessee, Florida, Arkansas, and Louisville fans, maybe.

But do you really think Wildcat supporters sat in the stands in Lexington last night and thought, "Man, I'm having a great time watching my eight-time national championship-winning program need a miracle to avoid what might be the worst loss in school history?"

Naturally, Pope got cooked over an open flame for this answer by both Kentucky fans and rivals alike.

I know I've been tough on Pope before, but stuff like this makes him hard to defend.

Kentucky fans were ready to get rid of John Calipari every season he failed to make the Sweet 16 towards the end there. I imagine those days feel halcyon by comparison.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

After Pope's eventful spring, in which he lost out on top recruit Tyran Stokes and had a disastrous Q&A on social media, I suggested he lie low for a bit and do some soul-searching while the fanbase cooled down.

Not only did he not do that, he just turned the temperature up even higher on his already flaming-hot seat.

I don't envy anyone who decides to be the head coach at Kentucky. That place is a pressure cooker and a thankless job at that.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

But Pope is doing himself no favors by being this tone-deaf.

Either hire a PR team or start winning some tournament games, Mark, because this isn't going to get any better as it stands right now.

item.title: Built from Scratch: How a meteorologist built a better umbrella
item.description: Rick Reichmuth, after 19 years as a Fox meteorologist, turned his sights on creating the perfect umbrella. Now, Weatherman sells five categories of umbrellas, ponchos, hats and more.
item.content:encoded:
Rick Reichmuth didn’t set out to start a business. He just wanted a better umbrella.

After 19 years as a Fox meteorologist, he knew how to predict the weather, yet he still couldn't find an umbrella that could survive it.

Staring at racks of umbrellas on the streets of New York City, he was struck by a glaring gap in the market: While categories like bandages and tissues had iconic, trusted household names, buying an umbrella was a total gamble.

CEO SUNDAY: ARMY VETERAN TURNED HEALTH TECH BOSS CALLS SUPPORT FOR THOSE WHO SERVED A ‘SACRED OBLIGATION’

After searching for a standout umbrella brand and coming up empty, he asked himself, "Why not create my own?" 

Nobody knows the elements better than a meteorologist, and with that, Weatherman was born.

Reichmuth started by taking apart hundreds of umbrellas in his New York City apartment. His goal was simple: He wanted to reverse-engineer how they worked, pinpoint why they failed and establish the blueprint for a truly great umbrella.

Armed with that research, he teamed up with an industrial designer friend to build a model that was strong, durable and built to withstand the elements.

CEO SUNDAY: AVELO AIRLINES CEO REVEALS THE HABIT HE CREDITS FOR HIS SUCCESS

Yet, despite a lengthy career in meteorology, nothing had prepared him for the ins and outs of running a business. Reichmuth remembers looking at the very first Weatherman prototype and thinking, "Wow, I think the hard part is finally over." 

As it turned out, the work was just beginning.

Running a small business tested Reichmuth in ways forecasting never did. He said it was a journey marked by steep trials and hard-earned lessons that he still calls the hardest thing he's ever done.

When Weatherman debuted in 2017, the lineup consisted of just two designs: a collapsible model and a stick umbrella. 

BUILT FROM SCRATCH: HOW A RENTED KITCHEN AND HAND-SQUEEZED FRUIT BECAME A VERSATILE MIXER

Both have since been retired, a testament to how relentlessly the brand has refined and upgraded its engineering over the last nine years. 

Entering a new industry without a product development background was intimidating, and early missteps hit hard. 

"Early on, a failure or setback could really knock me down," Reichmuth admits. "Sometimes I'd spend weeks feeling stuck, second-guessing decisions or worrying about what went wrong. That paralysis often became a bigger problem than the original mistake." 

Over time, learning to absorb those blows became Weatherman's greatest catalyst for growth. Today, Reichmuth caps his frustration at a few hours before pivoting back to problem-solving. 

"Admitting what you don't know is actually one of the most valuable things you can do," he says. "Once you accept that failure is normal — not something to be ashamed of — it becomes a whole lot easier to keep moving forward."

The ultimate validation didn't come from TV ratings; it came on the crowded sidewalks of New York. 

"I'd be walking around and suddenly see someone carrying one of our umbrellas," Reichmuth says. "That never gets old."

BUILT FROM SCRATCH: HOW A FAMILY TURNED CRAFT BEER INTO A HOLIDAY TRADITION

The sweetest moments, however, are the ones where customers praise the gear without any idea who he is. "They hadn't bought it because they'd seen me on television," he points out. "They bought it because a friend recommended it, or they discovered it online, or they'd heard it was a great umbrella."

For an entrepreneur who started by tearing apart umbrellas in his apartment, earning that pure, organic trust was everything. 

Today, with Weatherman expanding and solidly profitable over the last few years, the journey has more than paid off.

What separates Weatherman from the sea of disposable umbrellas? Engineering. Armed with heavy-duty fiberglass frames and water-repellent recycled fabric, the canopies are wind-tunnel tested to withstand gusts of up to 55 mph. 

They double as sun protection with built-in UPF 50+, and feature smooth auto-open mechanisms to spare users the classic rain-soaked struggle. 

CEO SUNDAY: ATOMIC WINGS CEO SHARES HIS JOURNEY FROM WALL STREET TO THE RESTAURANT BUSINESS

But the true differentiator is how Weatherman approaches design: by use case. Recognizing that a city commuter has different needs than a backcountry hiker or a weekend golfer, the brand organizes its lineup into distinct categories like Walk, Trek, Travel, Golf and Kids — outfitting each with specialized features like reflective trim or pocket-friendly sizing to match real-world habits. 

Today, Weatherman has expanded into sun shirts and ponchos for adults, kids and even pets — designed for real-life moments like youth soccer games or unexpected vacation downpours. 

Recognizing that not everyone wants to splurge on rain gear they hope to rarely use, Reichmuth and his team are developing a more affordable sister brand. 

Set to debut in 2027, it will bring Weatherman's signature thoughtful engineering to a wider, budget-conscious audience.

Still, one thing is for sure: Forecasts aren’t always certain, but Reichmuth’s goal is to help people stay prepared when conditions take an unexpected turn.

Pick the right umbrella for you, whether you're hiking, hitting the golf course or just walking to work.

item.description: Pilots, a former FAA official and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy explain the nationwide ground stop, detailing the telecom overload, 48-hour recovery and funding push.
item.content:encoded:
A former top FAA official who helped shut down New York airspace on 9/11 urged Congress to fund an overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system after equipment problems led to a nationwide ground stop.

Speaking on "Fox & Friends Weekend" on Saturday, former FAA air traffic senior executive Mike McCormick said Friday's outage highlighted the challenge of updating the agency's aging technology.

"It is always a challenge to do any modernization, update or technical refresh into the FAA's air traffic control system. It's similar to if you're going to change a tire on a car while it's still moving down the road," McCormick said while discussing the outage.

"The newer technology overwhelmed the pre-existing technology, and it led to the overload of the switching and associated software in the telecommunications system," he added. "And that led to communication problems, and then eventually the nationwide shutdown."

THOUSANDS OF FLIGHTS CANCELED AFTER LONGEST NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP IN 25 YEARS ROCKS US AIRPORTS

McCormick said he supports funding initiatives aimed at upgrading the nation's air traffic control system, emphasizing that the technology must meet both current and future demands.

NBA AND NHL TEAMS BATTLE DELAYS AS NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP DISRUPTS WEEKEND SPORTS TRAVEL

Although flights have resumed, McCormick warned that it could take days for air travel to return to normal.

"This will take several days in order to be able to get all of the aircraft, all the passengers, all the baggage, all of the flight crews, all where they need to be positioned to get the system up and running from early morning through the evening," he said. "So I would predict at least 48 hours in order to restore this completely."

At a Saturday news conference, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the outage began when a contractor performing routine maintenance at a remote FAA facility attempted to replace outdated copper lines with fiber-optic cables.

Duffy said a replacement router installed during the work flooded the agency's telecommunications network, triggering radar and radio instability. Duffy and Bedford said investigators found no evidence of a cyberattack.

FAA BREAKS CONTROLLER HIRING RECORD AFTER CHIEF WARNED SYSTEM WAS 'CHRONICALLY UNDERSTAFFED'

"Many of our contractors, many of our partners, they take our money, and they provide really poor service to us. Full stop," Duffy said, adding that he plans to submit a detailed funding request to Congress covering telecommunications upgrades and improvements to aging runways and control towers.

"This was an FAA system that didn't meet the moment, our contractor didn't meet the moment or the equipment didn't meet the moment, and caused the outages," Duffy said.

WHEN AIRLINE PILOTS SAY THERE ARE SAFETY ISSUES, WE NEED POLICYMAKERS TO LISTEN AND ACT

Despite the widespread disruptions, aviation experts said the decision to halt flights demonstrated the safety measures built into the nation's air traffic system.

Josh Schirard, a commercial pilot and head of law enforcement at Byrna Technologies, said the incident showed that the aviation system prioritizes passenger safety over convenience. He praised pilots, air traffic controllers and flight crews for safely bringing aircraft to the ground.

"The big takeaway from what we saw over the last 24 hours really is for the American traveler, how safe our air system really is, and yesterday was a great illustration of that," Schirard said.

"Through the safety of the infrastructure that does exist – through the pilots, the crew, the controllers, through the airplanes themselves and really the redundancy of protocols and practices that are in place – that all combined is what allowed us to take 3,500 planes in a matter of hours and over a million travelers and get them on the ground safely," he said.

Scott Pattillo, a retired United Airlines pilot, said his initial reaction to a nationwide ground stop would have been disbelief if he had been flying at the time.

"Well, first thing I think is, 'Holy crap, is this real? Is this really happening on a Friday the 13th?' And second thing, it harps back to 9/11, and we all remember what that was like, especially if we were working and flying during that time," he said. "So the first thing, as a pilot, is I'm not [going to] panic."

Pattillo explained that, based on his understanding, the outage disrupted radar data and radio communications for high-altitude air traffic controllers. Airport towers and controllers handling arriving aircraft, however, relied on separate technology that was not affected by the same outage.

Pattillo said that distinction allowed pilots already in the air to continue along their assigned routes and safely reach their destinations.

"As a pilot, you have to remain predictable," Pattillo said. "And you're trained under certain scenarios what to do. And the best thing to do is continue on that path."

Pattillo also defended the decision to ground flights nationwide, calling it "absolutely" the right move.

"When you start to lose a level of safety that we all expect, then yeah, that was exactly the right call, to start shutting down the airspace," he said.

item.title: DEPROGRAMMED: A 'kind offer' of death sent this couple running from universal health care
item.description: Donovan James calls Canada's MAID program "evil" after his wife Kristin says she received end-of-life info before even getting an oncology appointment.
item.content:encoded:
Kristin Logan and Donovan James say they moved to Canada with their sights set on the financial and medical benefits of publicly funded healthcare — but say they encountered a "dystopian" system that offered medically assisted death before cancer treatment, prompting them to return to the United States.

"Canada has been slowly sliding into an entire dystopian situation. The way they've expanded the MAID system is frightening. It was never supposed to be used this way, to be offered so easily and so upfront when a person gets sick. I think it's evil," James told Fox News Digital.

"It was the most heartbreaking experience, to basically be set up to die. And if I wanted to live, I had to take my life into my own hands and leave the country. It's pretty dystopian to think about now, to get information about ways that I can end my life and what the end of my life looks like before I'd even gotten an oncology appointment," Logan continued.

SON SOUNDS ALARM AFTER FATHER'S MEDICALLY ASSISTED DEATH IN CANADA: WAY PAST APPROPRIATE'

Logan said she was first diagnosed in September 2023, leaving Canada later that month to get initial treatment. She later had a bowel obstruction in March 2024. She had to leave the country again, and then returned in April 2024 before the cancer returned in December 2024.

The couple decided to leave Canada in January 2025 and officially moved back to the United States in May of that year.

MAID — Canada's medical assistance in dying program — is described by Health Canada as "a health service that allows eligible people to receive help from a medical practitioner in ending their life."

According to Kristin and Donovan, MAID was the best initial solution Canada offered to her upon her diagnosis. The Atlantic has reported that MAID now accounts for about one in 20 deaths in Canada, "surpassing countries where assisted dying has been legal for far longer," with some raising concerns the program has become too expansive.

"They should be focusing on treating people and helping people live, but instead they've expanded the system as a kind offer because they pretty much assume you're going to die," he continued.

GRANDDAUGHTER SAYS GRANDMA REJECTED MAID BEFORE LETHAL PROCEDURE, ‘I DON’T WANT THE DEATH SHOT’

James, a Canadian citizen living in the United States with a green card, is the husband of Kristin Logan, a U.S. Air Force veteran who has stage four ovarian cancer.

They moved to Canada to get ahead of potential financial difficulty in the case of a future medical crisis to avoid "ever going bankrupt" — a hypothetical that crashed into reality following Kristin’s three separate travels back to America in a desperate fight for her life due to high wait times and lack of resources available in the Canadian healthcare system.

Logan had multiple emergencies and hospital trips during her time in Canada when a second bowel obstruction shifted her and her family’s fight or flight into overdrive to find a plan to save her life.

CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’

James said Canadian medical providers told the family there were "no plan[s] to operate on her," that a hospital helicopter was unavailable for a transfer to Vancouver and that a doctor advised Logan to "leave the country" if she had the means. The family ultimately traveled to the United States for treatment.

"Kristin was deteriorating really fast… Ultimately, we had to pull the plug and take her off the machines at the hospital and risk everything to put her in the car, drive all the way down Vancouver Island, sail across the ocean straight on a ferry, continue down over the border back into Seattle to get her immediate emergency surgery," James said.

"The surgeon said had she waited another day, she would have gone septic and died in Canada," he continued.

THE MEDICARE FOR ALL TRADE-OFFS SOCIALISTS AREN'T TALKING ABOUT, ACCORDING TO EXPERTS

"[It] was devastating and shocking. I was only 43 years old when I was given this diagnosis… It made me very angry that I had been chasing this disease for nine months and had been stymied at just about every turn by the healthcare system in Canada," Logan continued.

"Americans don't get enough Canadian news to know just how much Canadian healthcare has declined over the last couple [of] decades. It's always had this problem, but now it's just so much more worse and dystopian with this M.A.I.D. program that they've introduced - and it was never supposed to be used this way," James said.

British Columbia has announced an expansion of services for women with gynecological cancer. According to the Fraser Institute's 2025 report, the reported median wait time for gynecology was 25 weeks from referral by a general practitioner to consultation with a specialist, followed by 15.6 weeks from specialist consultation to treatment.

Health Canada, the lead federal department for the MAID program in Canada, did not immediately respond to Fox Digital's request for comment.

item.title: FAA ground stop forces changes for TNA Wrestling's Destination X pay-per-view
item.description: TNA Wrestling's Destination X in Edmonton faces lineup changes after the FAA nationwide ground stop stranded wrestlers trying to reach the event.
item.content:encoded:
Total Nonstop Action Wrestling’s (TNA) Destination X pay-per-view was among the events affected by the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) nationwide ground stop, the company said.

Destination X is set to take place in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, on Sunday. But the FAA’s decision to halt flights for several hours on Friday caused issues for pro wrestlers who were set to perform at the event. TNA said the show will still go on at Edmonton Expo Center but there will be some changes to the lineup.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

"After a wild 24 hours, we are really excited for the returning Destination X on Sunday afternoon," TNA Wrestling president Carlos Silva said in a statement posted to X. "As always, card subject to change - and yes, there will be changes to the originally scheduled lineup, forced by travel predicaments that are affecting travelers around the world."

Silva said at least two TNA stars offered to take a short flight and then drive over 600 miles just to make the show.

"That said, I'm proud of the way all at TNA Wrestling are banding together to deliver what will be a great show. In fact, we have two stars offering to take a short flight within the U.S., then drive more than 600 miles, just because they want to be a part of Destination X," Silva added.

LIVE COVERAGE: THOUSANDS OF FLIGHTS CANCELED AFTER LONGEST NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP IN 25 YEARS ROCKS US AIRPORTS

TNA vowed that the "show must – and will – go on."

The changes have yet to be announced.

Sunday’s Destination X is the first time the specific pay-per-view has been held since 2017.

Destination X has been a staple show of TNA since the 2010s. The event itself features some of the high-flyers of the X Division. One of the premier matches of the event is the Ultimate X match, which forces the competing wrestlers to navigate a rope that hangs over the four corners of the ring. Usually, a championship is hung in the center.

Ultimate X matches for future TNA Knockouts World Championship and X Division Championship shots were set to take place on Sunday’s card.

item.title: Shane Gillis says he promised 'no controversy' before 'SNL' monologue that sparked backlash
item.description: Shane Gillis said on "The Joe Rogan Experience" that "Saturday Night Live" producers didn't approve his monologue he called a "solid C minus."
item.content:encoded:
Comedian Shane Gillis said he promised "Saturday Night Live" producers "no controversy" before delivering a monologue that sparked a backlash over his jokes about women’s revealing gym attire.

"Not to defend SNL, they don't approve it. I mean, they could shut it down," Gillis said on the podcast "The Joe Rogan Experience."

"But you don't write your set and give it to them," he added. "Unless you’re not a comedian. I’m sure non-comics, they write the set for them. They have writers that write the monologue for them."

JOE ROGAN DEFENDS SHANE GILLIS FROM 'WORD POLICE' AFTER SNL JOKE SPARKS LIBERAL UPROAR

"The funniest part was ... they were like, ‘What’s going on with the monologue?’ And I was like, ‘It’s not great, but I don’t say anything bad.’ The whole time, I was like, ‘Fellas, I’m giving you a solid C-minus of a monologue, but I promise there’s no controversy. I’m calling myself fat for f---ing 10 minutes. That’s it.'"

Gillis, 38, drew criticism from celebrities including actor Dan Levy and former "SNL" cast member Ego Nwodim after joking during his Oct. 10 hosting appearance that women at the gym "dress like whores."

'SNL' CAST MEMBER MICHAEL CHE SHRUGS OFF SHANE GILLIS' MONOLOGUE JOKE SAYING, 'THAT'S COMEDY'

"I haven’t been to the gym in so long. I didn’t know women just dress like whores now?" Gillis said during the opening monologue.

"Look, I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe [it]. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. You’ve seen the shorts? They’re those neon, like, artificial bait-colored [shorts], and the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don’t look! You’re not allowed to look."

CORNELL PROTESTERS SWARM CAMPUS TO SUPPORT JANE DOE, CALL FOR UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT'S RESIGNATION

Jason Mudd, CEO of Axia Public Relations, talked to Fox News Digital about Gillis speaking out on the controversy.

"If Shane Gillis were my public relations client, I'd advise him to acknowledge the people who were offended before he explains his intent," he suggested.

"The people who book his next gig may not hear the podcast," Mudd added. "They tend to watch how he handles the aftermath. If he cares and wants as many opportunities as possible, he might need to pivot. Maybe he doesn’t care. If that’s on brand, he can stay himself." 

Carvey said on his "Fly on the Wall" podcast with David Spade that he did not understand the controversy and viewed Gillis' remarks as a joke.

"I just didn't understand the kerfuffle," he said. "Only 'cause to me, I just saw it as what we call – I'll just say it – a joke," he added.

Fox News Digital reached out to NBC for comment. 

Fox News Digital's Lauryn Overhultz contributed to this report.

item.title: Justice Alito warns America must preserve 3 core principles regardless of country’s ‘atmosphere’
item.description: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito outlined three principles he says Americans must always prioritize amid the 2026 midterms and the Iran War.
item.content:encoded:
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito recently laid out three principles Americans must cling to to ensure the integrity of the republic: freedom of speech, religious liberty and racial equality.

"I'm not saying we're entering the dark age, but these are things that we have to preserve no matter what the atmosphere is in the country or the world at the time," Alito said during a fireside chat with Mollie Hemingway, editor-in-chief at the Federalist, which followed the Antonin Scalia Memorial Dinner at the 2026 National Lawyer's Convention in Washington D.C.

The remarks come on the heels of the blue tsunami of the 2026 midterms, with Republicans losing 42 House seats and eight Senate seats, with the Alaska U.S. Senate race still uncalled. Democrats are set to take control of Congress with eight lawmakers backed by the Democratic Socialists of America. Both incoming and returning members have pressed for investigations and subpoenas targeting President Donald Trump and his administration.

DEMOCRATS SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN

Alito's remarks also come amid the ongoing Iran war, which has destabilized oil supply chains across the globe, causing the price of goods and gas to jump.

The 76-year-old jurist said preserving freedom of speech is paramount, warning that "you cannot have Democratic self-fulfillment if you cannot have robust free speech."

"Even speech that is hurtful to some of the people who hear what is being said," Alito said.

He also stressed the importance of freedom of religion, even as the Supreme Court is set to rule on at least two major cases this term centered on religious freedom: St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy and Grand v. City of University Heights.

SUPREME COURT OFFERS SUPPORT FOR CATHOLIC PRESCHOOLS CHALLENGING STATE FUNDING REQUIREMENTS

"I think that we have placed religious liberty on a sounder footing than it was on 20, 25 years ago," Alito said.

"Religious liberty is central to human dignity, and in a society that is as religiously diverse as this country, we've got people who adhere to practically every religion that exists in the world," Alito continued. "We are not going to be able to get along, I think, amicably, productively, if we don't respect everybody's right to follow whatever religion they want, or for people of faith, they're also free to do that."

"That's essential," Alito said.

He rounded off his trifecta by saying that America must maintain racial equality, declaring it "essential for our pluralistic society."

FEDERAL JUDGE TOSSES TRUMP ADMIN HARVARD ADMISSIONS LAWSUIT, LEAVES DOOR OPEN TO FUTURE CHALLENGE

"That is the principle that Dr. Martin Luther King famously articulated in his speech at the Lincoln Memorial, where he said he looked forward to the day when children would be judged by the content of their character and not by the color of their skin," Alito said.

"If we don't hold to that principle, then I think the society is going to start to come apart," Alito said.

The Supreme Court agreed in October to hear Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education this term, a challenge brought by parents of Asian American students alleging that a Maryland school district’s admissions policies unlawfully discriminate despite appearing race-neutral.

Alito mentioned the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, which ended affirmative action in college admissions, as among the most consequential rulings from the Supreme Court in the past few decades.

TRUMP CHEERS ALITO STAYING FOR ANOTHER SUPREME COURT TERM: 'ONE OF THE GREATEST OF ALL TIME'

Alito's discussion comes as questions swirl about his possible plans to retire. In a Bloomberg article published after the midterms, Alito said that the Democrats' sweep did not change his plans to stay on the Supreme Court.

Alito, nominated by President George W. Bush, has served on the bench since 2006.

"With those, with those 20 years, I jumped to 42nd in the the list of all-time service by Supreme Court justices," Alito said.

item.title: US reportedly loses longstanding measles elimination status as cases surge nationwide
item.description: PAHO has reportedly revoked the U.S. measles elimination status held since 2000, with over 5,412 confirmed cases in 2026 signaling continuous spread.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. has reportedly lost its measles-elimination status after 26 years, The Wall Street Journal reported Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.

Loss of this status means measles is spreading continuously within the U.S. again, with the same chain of transmission persisting for at least 12 months, according to the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO).

PAHO had planned to announce the determination publicly on Tuesday, Nov. 17, according to KFF Health News, which separately reported the decision, citing researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations.

WISCONSIN INFANT DIES OF MEASLES AS STATE SEES FIRST DEATH FROM DISEASE SINCE 1990

The country has held elimination status since 2000. Isolated cases and shorter outbreaks can still occur without forfeiting that status.

PAHO’s independent regional verification commission reviewed countries’ elimination status during its Nov. 10-13 meeting in Washington, D.C.

The U.S. reported 5,412 confirmed measles cases in 2026 through Nov. 12, more than double the 2,289 cases reported in all of 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Dr. Stephanie Widmer, a New York City-based emergency medicine physician and Fox News medical contributor, said the loss of measles elimination status is a "public health setback," emphasizing the danger posed by the infection.

"Measles isn’t just a childhood rash. It can cause pneumonia, brain inflammation, permanent neurological damage and death," she told Fox News Digital on Saturday. "As an emergency physician, I can tell you these complications are not something we should ever take lightly."

AMERICAN VACCINES THAT TRANSFORMED PUBLIC HEALTH OVER 250 YEARS: 'OUTWEIGHS HARM'

"Losing elimination status doesn’t mean the vaccine stopped working," she went on. "It means we no longer have enough protection in some communities to prevent sustained transmission."

The doctor emphasized that infants who are too young to be vaccinated and people with compromised immune systems are "paying the price for gaps in community immunity."

The loss of measles elimination status "signals that the virus is spreading continuously and that too many people remain unprotected," according to the American Academy of Family Physicians.

"It does not mean the MMR vaccine has stopped working," the AAFP said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. "It means we must restore confidence in the safety and efficacy of life-saving public health tools."

Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst, said the change reflects transmission within the country.

"The result of losing this status is a recognition that not all spread is due to travel from overseas," he told Fox News Digital.

Siegel also called for bringing vaccination services directly to communities with low vaccination rates.

"I think one of the solutions here is for health authorities to send vaccine trucks and clinics to areas where vaccine noncompliance most exists," he said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Measles is highly contagious, infecting up to nine in 10 people without immunity who are close to an infected person, the CDC states. The virus can linger in the air for up to two hours after that person leaves.

Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine have been shown to be about 97% effective at preventing the disease.

The CDC recommends that children receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, with the first given at 12 to 15 months and the second at 4 to 6 years.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Most adults without evidence of immunity need one MMR dose, while certain higher-risk adults need two, according to the agency. People with two appropriately spaced doses generally do not need a measles booster.

"Restoring elimination status requires an organized and sustained response that includes increased support for state and local health departments, timelier surveillance and communications, clear information for families and an easier path to vaccination," the AAFP said.

Fox News Digital reached out to PAHO and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services requesting comment.

item.title: NFL official Don Willard will referee two games in one day after FAA ground stop disrupts travel, league says
item.description: NFL official Don Willard will referee two games in one day, driving 110 miles from Indianapolis to Cincinnati after the FAA ground stop hit Week 10.
item.content:encoded:
The FAA lifted its nationwide ground stop on Friday night, but the impact will be felt on football fields Sunday.

The NFL announced that it had to adjust its officiating assignments for Week 10 games, reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns. One referee, Don Willard, will officiate two games on the same day.

"The changes will necessitate that three backup referees – umpires Barry Anderson and Duane Heydt and side judge Don Willard – will work as referees in the following games:

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Carolina-New Orleans – Duane Heydt

Jacksonville-Tennessee – Barry Anderson

Miami-Indianapolis and Pittsburgh-Cincinnati – Don Willard."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Shawn Smith was initially scheduled to work the Carolina Panthers-New Orleans Saints game, Alex Moore was set for the Jacksonville Jaguars- Tennessee Titans matchup, Carl Cheffers was going to referee the Miami Dolphins-Indianapolis Colts game, and Clete Blakeman was supposed to referee the Pittsburgh Steelers-Cincinnati Bengals game.

REDZONE HOST SCOTT HANSON DEFENDS NFL OFFICIATING, CALLS LEAGUE 'BEST OFFICIATED' IN AMERICA

Willard will begin the day in Indianapolis for Colts-Dolphins at 1 p.m. ET and then drive roughly 110 miles to Cincinnati to referee Steelers-Bengals at 8:20 p.m. ET. It is unknown whether Willard will be the first referee ever to work two games in one day.

Willard has been an NFL official for nine seasons.

In the NFL’s announcement, the league said each of its 17 officiating crews has a designated backup who is trained throughout the season to fill in when needed.

The FAA’s nationwide ground stop was just the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. More than 2,000 flights were canceled, forcing college football teams to scramble ahead of Saturday’s games.

item.title: Princess Diana’s legendary White House dance with John Travolta almost didn’t happen
item.description: Princess Diana danced with Clint Eastwood, Tom Selleck and Ronald Reagan that evening, but it took coaxing to get John Travolta onto the floor.
item.content:encoded:
John Travolta had all the right moves, but when the chance to dance with Princess Diana came along, even Hollywood's smoothest dancer got cold feet.

The Princess of Wales and the actor lit up the White House ballroom in 1985, creating one of the most unforgettable moments in royal and Hollywood history. Diana was attending a White House dinner hosted by President Ronald Reagan and first lady Nancy Reagan when she took a spin with the heartthrob.

More than four decades later, their legendary dance is being celebrated at "Princess Diana: Love, Life, Legacy — A Life of Giving," an exhibition at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library in Simi Valley, California. More than 700 artifacts connected to Diana's life are on display.

PRINCESS DIANA, HOT DOGS AND A PRESIDENTIAL MATCHMAKING ATTEMPT: ICONIC ROYAL VISITS TO AMERICA

The collection, presented through a partnership between the Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute (RRPFI) and Renae Plant's Princess Diana Museum, features the velvet gown designed by Victor Edelstein that Diana wore that night.

But the iconic dance nearly didn't happen.

"In preparation for the state dinner, the Marine Band that was going to perform the music during the dinner was told to rehearse music from 'Saturday Night Fever,'" Melissa Giller, chief marketing and cultural programming officer at RRPFI, told Fox News Digital.

WATCH: PRINCESS DIANA'S ICONIC DANCE WITH TRAVOLTA GETS NEW SPOTLIGHT

"The social secretary, Gahl Burt, she orchestrated it after speaking with Mrs. Reagan that after the dancing began, Gahl would walk up to John Travolta and tap him on the shoulder and encourage him to have a dance with Princess Diana," Giller said. "Now through the whole evening, Princess Diana danced with Ronald Reagan. She danced with Clint Eastwood. She danced with Tom Selleck and many others."

But when it came time for Travolta to step onto the dance floor with Diana, he needed some coaxing.

"When it was time, Gahl Burt walked up to John Travolta and tapped him on the shoulder," Giller said. "He was actually a bit hesitant. He didn't know if it was something he should do. But after some encouragement, he went up and asked the princess to dance."

Travolta mustered the courage and approached Diana. The two then waltzed across the checkered floor to music from "Saturday Night Fever."

"They ended up dancing for 15 minutes," Giller said with a smile.

"Every presidential library archive has a photo that's the most requested by the public. President Nixon's library is the photo of Elvis meeting President Nixon. And one of our most requested photos is the one of Princess Diana dancing with John Travolta."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Travolta later admitted he was nervous before approaching Diana.

"I didn't think they'd ask me to dance with her," he told Esquire Mexico in 2021. "I had the great privilege and honor of doing so, and I thought, 'There must be a reason for doing this and I better give it my all.’ That meant lead the dance well and make sure we had fun. That was the easy part, but just the fact of greeting Diana appropriately, being confident and asking her to dance was a complicated task."

The "Grease" star also recalled how special it was to dance with Diana.

"Think of the setting. We were at the White House. It's midnight. The stage is like a dream. I approach her, touch her elbow, invite her to dance," he said. "She spins around and gives me that captivating smile, just a little sad, and accepts my invitation. And there we were, dancing together as if it were a fairytale."

In the 2021 interview, Travolta also recalled his disbelief over the once-in-a-lifetime encounter.

"Who could imagine that something like this is going to happen to you one day? I was smart enough to register it in my memory as a very special, magical moment."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Travolta also told Dutch television station Één that it was Nancy who told him Diana wanted to dance with him.

"[She] said, 'It is her wish,'" the actor recalled. "At midnight, I had to tap her on her shoulder, and I had to say, 'Would you care to dance?' She turned around and dipped her head in that Lady Diana way, and we were off for 15 minutes dancing."

"I'll never forget it," he continued. "I'm so honored that I was able to experience this, and I know for a fact that it was her highlight of being in the United States; it was her favorite moment. So I feel I made her life better, she made my life better, and I'm very sorry that she's not here."

During a 2016 appearance on "Good Morning America," Travolta was asked if there was anything from the 1980s that he'd like to bring back to the 2010s. He said he'd love to dance with Diana again.

"That was one of the highlights of my life, so that's probably the best moment of the '80s."

Giller noted that the Prince and Princess of Wales maintained a close friendship with the Reagans.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"When Princess Diana got married to Prince Charles, Ronald Reagan, as President of the United States, could not go because the assassination attempt happened a few months ago and he was [still] recovering," Giller explained. "So, Mrs. Reagan went on behalf of President Reagan, as well as the United States. And I think that sort of bonded her with Princess Diana, although of course, Mrs. Reagan was much older than Princess Diana."

"They shared a kinship, especially once Princess Diana became a mother," Giller said. "You can see that in [their] letters and their relationship."

The exhibition features letters Nancy and Diana wrote to each other over the years, as well as gifts the Reagans received from the Prince and Princess of Wales.

Giller said the exhibition aims to show visitors the woman behind the royal title, highlighting Diana's humanitarian work and influence beyond her relationship with the Reagans.

"This isn't just an exhibition about dresses and shoes and jewelry," she said. "This is an exhibition about a woman who truly cared about her family, about her people, about all people, not just those in Europe, but around the world."

The exhibition, which opened Nov. 7, runs through May 31, 2027.

item.title: Hugh Jackman, Sutton Foster enjoy romantic beach day in Australia
item.description: Hugh Jackman and Sutton Foster were photographed sharing a kiss and playing Frisbee at Sydney's Bondi Beach.
item.content:encoded:
Hugh Jackman and Sutton Foster enjoyed a recent trip to the beach.

The couple was photographed at Bondi Beach in Sydney, Australia, after the actor recently celebrated his 58th birthday.

In the photos, Jackman and Foster are seen walking along the shore and relaxing on the sand.

item.title: New prostate cancer guidelines urge men to start screening at specific age
item.description: The American Cancer Society's new guidelines now recommend PSA blood tests every two years for men 50-69, with Black men urged to start annual screening at 45.
item.content:encoded:
The American Cancer Society is recommending regular prostate cancer screening starting at age 50 for men at average risk under updated guidelines released Nov. 12.

The update shifts from emphasizing individual decisions about screening to explicitly recommending regular testing for eligible men.

The new guidelines call for PSA testing every two years for average-risk men ages 50 through 69. Black men should begin annual screening at 45, regardless of family history. Other men with a father, brother or son diagnosed with prostate cancer should also begin at 45, with the frequency depending on their family history.

JOE BIDEN SHARES HEALTH UPDATE AFTER PROSTATE CANCER DIAGNOSIS WHILE ISSUING WARNING TO OTHERS

Men ages 70 to 74 should discuss whether to continue screening with their doctors; routine screening is not recommended at 75 and older.

Prostate cancer is the second-leading cause of cancer death among U.S. men. 

For disease that has not spread beyond the prostate or nearby areas, the five-year relative survival rate is nearly 100%, according to the American Cancer Society.

"Men think it is going to happen to someone else," Dr. Ash Tewari, chair of the Milton and Carroll Petrie Department of Urology at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai Medical Center in New York City, told Fox News.

MAN GOES TO DOCTOR TO PROVE HE’S 'IN PERFECT SHAPE,' TEST REVEALS SHOCKING DIAGNOSIS

The doctor, who has performed more than 10,000 prostate cancer operations, said the success rate of treating patients is exceedingly high, but that many men still need to be nudged to get screened.

A prostate cancer screening involves a simple blood test for PSA, which measures the level of prostate-specific antigen, the protein produced by normal and cancerous cells in the prostate gland.

Under the updated guidelines, a PSA level of 3 ng/mL or higher in men younger than 70 warrants a repeat test to confirm the result. There are other explanations for higher PSA levels beyond the existence of prostate cancer, such as an enlarged prostate, inflammation or an infection.

CANCER DOCTOR REVEALS 5 HABITS THAT MAY REDUCE DISEASE RISK AND IMPROVE OUTCOMES

Screening can also identify slow-growing cancers that may never cause harm. The society recommends discussing screening’s benefits and possible harms with a healthcare provider and offering close monitoring as an initial approach for low-risk cancers.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"We know how to cure 95% of them," said Tewari, referring to prostate cancer patients. "I can operate, we have developed medications … to get to them in time, my approach is very simple: Go right where they are."

To reach more men, Tewari and Mount Sinai have created mobile prostate cancer screening vehicles that are deployed in neighborhoods so men can be examined where they live.

The first bus, the Mount Sinai Robert F. Smith Mobile Prostate Cancer Screening Unit, was sent out in New York City in 2022. Last month, another bus was deployed to the Atlanta Falcons-Chicago Bears game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta. The Winship Cancer Institute at Emory University offered free screenings in partnership with the Atlanta Falcons during the game.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Tewari and Mount Sinai are engaged in other ways to get the word out to men.

Last month, actress Brooke Shields joined Tewari and directed a public service announcement advocating screening and early detection. The goal is to screen more than one million men for prostate cancer under Tewari's Million Strong Men Initiative.

"We need to be able to talk about ...down there," a son says to his father in the PSA video.

"I never got to have the talk with my dad early enough," says Shields in the video. Her father, Frank, died of prostate cancer in 2003 at 61 years old.

"Prostate cancer is treatable when detected early," she adds.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Prostate cancer is often a disease that families don't talk about until there is a reason to," said Tewari. "We want to change that. Starting the conversation early can give men an opportunity to learn about their risk, talk with their doctors about screening and act when appropriate."

Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers in men. The ACS estimates that more than 333,000 men in the U.S. will be diagnosed in 2026, and about 36,000 will die from the disease.
